questions.question: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error: (1) Scarcely the newly appointed Chancellor had delivered his inaugural address concerning the revitalization of the national economy / (2) when a sudden plummet in the value of the currency triggered a widespread panic (3) / among the international investors who had previously viewed the region / (4) as a bastion of financial stability and untapped industrial potential.
questions.questionHtml:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(1) Scarcely the newly appointed Chancellor had delivered his inaugural address concerning the revitalization of the national economy / (2) when a sudden plummet in the value of the currency triggered a widespread panic (3) / among the international investors who had previously viewed the region / (4) as a bastion of financial stability and untapped industrial potential.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. Scarcely the newly appointed Chancellor had delivered his inaugural address .

Key Points

  • The sentence contains an error in the usage of the word "scarcely."
  • The correct phrase should be "Scarcely had the newly appointed Chancellor delivered his inaugural address."
  • When using "scarcely" at the beginning of a sentence, it is followed by an inverted word order (auxiliary verb + subject). This is a grammatical rule in formal English.

Correct sentence: Scarcely had the newly appointed Chancellor delivered his inaugural address concerning the revitalization of the national economy when a sudden plummet in the value of the currency triggered a widespread panic among the international investors who had previously viewed the region as a bastion of financial stability and untapped industrial potential..

Additional Information

  • Inversion after negative adverbs:
    • Negative adverbs like "scarcely," "hardly," "no sooner," and "rarely" require inversion when placed at the beginning of a sentence.
    • Example: "No sooner had she entered the room than everyone turned to look."
    • Reason: This is a formal construction used for emphasis.
  • Common Error:
    • Incorrect: "Scarcely the Chancellor had delivered his address."
    • Correct: "Scarcely had the Chancellor delivered his address."
    • Explanation: The auxiliary verb "had" must precede the subject "the Chancellor."

questions.question: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error: (1) The archaeological team, having spent over a decade excavating the subterranean ruins of the Mesoamerican city, / (2) was originally reported to discover the lost codices during the first phase of the project, / (3) although subsequent carbon dating revealed that the artifacts were placed there / (4) centuries after the civilization’s initial collapse.
questions.questionHtml:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(1) The archaeological team, having spent over a decade excavating the subterranean ruins of the Mesoamerican city, / (2) was originally reported to discover the lost codices during the first phase of the project, / (3) although subsequent carbon dating revealed that the artifacts were placed there / (4) centuries after the civilization’s initial collapse.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. was originally reported to discover.

Key Points

  • The phrase "was originally reported to discover" is incorrect because the verb "discover" is not appropriate in this context.
  • The correct verb form should be "was originally reported to have discovered," which aligns with proper grammatical structure.
  • "To have discovered" indicates that the reporting referred to a past event of discovery.

Correct sentence: The archaeological team, having spent over a decade excavating the subterranean ruins of the Mesoamerican city, was originally reported to have discovered the lost codices during the first phase of the project.

Additional Information

  • Reported Speech:
    • When reporting past events, the verb form often changes to reflect the completed action.
    • Example: "He is said to have won the race" (correct) versus "He is said to win the race" (incorrect).
  • Past Perfect Usage:
    • The past perfect tense ("to have discovered") is used to indicate that the discovery happened before another event in the past.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that rectifies the underlined group of words in the given sentence. The architect and myself, after having conferred with the structural engineers, decided that the cantilevered roof required additional reinforcement.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that rectifies the underlined group of words in the given sentence.

The architect and myself, after having conferred with the structural engineers, decided that the cantilevered roof required additional reinforcement.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. I, after having conferred .

Key Points

  • The phrase “The architect and myself” is grammatically incorrect because “myself” is a reflexive pronoun and cannot be used as a subject.
  • Reflexive pronouns are used for emphasis or when the subject and object of the sentence are the same, which is not the case here.
  • The correct pronoun to use in this context is “I,” as it is part of the subject of the sentence.

Correct sentence: The architect and I, after having conferred with the structural engineers, decided that the cantilevered roof required additional reinforcement.

Additional Information

  • Reflexive Pronouns:
    • Used when the subject and object are the same or to emphasize the subject.
    • Example: "I hurt myself." Here, “myself” refers back to the subject “I.”
  • Subject Pronouns:
    • Used as the subject of a sentence.
    • Example: "I went to the store." Here, “I” is the subject performing the action.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 Additional Information

The correct answer is 'Option 1'.
 
Key Points
  • Adroit Pivoting

  • Preservation of Patrimony
    • By monopolizing bishoprics, the elite sought to "preserve their patrimony" (inherited wealth) and "cultural hegemony." This suggests that protecting their own status was a higher priority than clinging to the failing central imperial government.
  • Continuity of Hierarchy
    • The passage emphasizes that the power structure didn't disappear; it simply changed its "locus" (location/center). The elites ensured their survival by integrating themselves into the most stable burgeoning institution: the Catholic Church.
Therefore, it can be inferred that the aristocracy prioritized the maintenance of their localized social power and wealth over loyalty to a failing secular imperial government.
 
Historical Context
  • Option 2: Incorrect; the Church was a vehicle for preserving their influence, not a weapon for dismantling the state.
  • Option 3: Incorrect; the Church became the vessel through which classical traditions were "seamlessly interwoven" into the medieval world.
  • Option 4: Incorrect; the passage states that localized agrarian economies were "remarkably resilient" rather than collapsing.

Key Points
  • Long-term Integration

  • The Foederati Model
    • The author cites the foederati system—land in exchange for service—as a primary example of mutually beneficial interdependence. This system transformed tribes into internal "sub-contractors" rather than external enemies.
  • Symbiotic Relationship
    • While the relationship is described as "occasionally volatile," the emphasis is on the symbiotic nature of their coexistence, where Germanic groups appropriated Roman administrative prestige to form successor states.
Therefore, the most logical conclusion is that the tribes were already heavily integrated into the empire's frameworks through mutually beneficial agreements.
 
Analysis of Contextual Clues
  • "Enmeshed": Suggests deep integration rather than isolation (refutes Option 1).
  • "Internal devolution": Indicates that change happened from within the system (supports Option 4).
  • "Appropriated the vestiges": Shows the tribes valued and used Roman structures (refutes Option 3).

questions.question: Which of the following cell organelles functions as a cytoplasmic framework, providing a surface for some of the biochemical activities of the cell?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following cell organelles functions as a cytoplasmic framework, providing a surface for some of the biochemical activities of the cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Endoplasmic Reticulum.

Key Points

  • The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranes within the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells that provides structural support and a surface for various biochemical processes.
  • It plays a crucial role in protein synthesis (in the rough ER) and lipid metabolism (in the smooth ER).
  • The rough ER is studded with ribosomes, making it the site for the synthesis of secretory and membrane-bound proteins.
  • The smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is involved in the synthesis of lipids, detoxification of harmful substances, and storage of calcium ions.
  • By providing a large surface area, the ER facilitates the compartmentalization of cellular processes, ensuring efficiency and organization within the cell.

Additional Information

  • Endoplasmic Reticulum Types:
    • The Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) is associated with ribosomes and participates in protein synthesis and folding.
    • The Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid biosynthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage.
  • Protein Synthesis: Proteins synthesized in the rough ER are transported to the Golgi apparatus for further modification and sorting.
  • Calcium Storage: The smooth ER in muscle cells (sarcoplasmic reticulum) stores and releases calcium ions, which are critical for muscle contraction.
  • Detoxification: The smooth ER in liver cells helps detoxify drugs and harmful chemicals by converting them into water-soluble compounds.
  • Golgi Apparatus Link: The ER works closely with the Golgi apparatus to transport proteins and lipids to their target destinations within or outside the cell.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are not a scalar quantity? 1. Mass 2. Entropy 3. Work 4. Force 5. Weight 6. Time 7. Density
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is/are not a scalar quantity?
1. Mass
2. Entropy
3. Work
4. Force
5. Weight
6. Time
7. Density
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 4 and 5.

Key Points

  • Force is a vector quantity as it has both magnitude and direction. It is represented mathematically as F = ma, where 'a' is the acceleration in a specific direction.
  • Weight is also a vector quantity because it acts in the direction of gravitational force. Weight is defined as W = mg, where 'g' is the acceleration due to gravity.
  • Scalar quantities, such as mass, entropy, work, time, and density, have only magnitude and no direction.
  • The distinction between scalar and vector quantities lies in whether the quantity has an associated direction or not.

Additional Information

  • Scalar Quantity: Quantities that are fully described by magnitude alone, such as mass, temperature, energy, and time.
  • Vector Quantity: Quantities that are described by both magnitude and direction, such as force, velocity, displacement, and acceleration.
  • Force: A vector quantity that represents the interaction between two objects. It is measured in Newtons (N) and has both magnitude and direction.
  • Weight: A specific type of force that represents the gravitational pull on an object. It is dependent on both the mass of the object and the gravitational field strength.
  • Work: A scalar quantity defined as the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force. Even though force is a vector, work is scalar since it depends only on the magnitude of the components.

questions.question: Which article was referred to by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the "Dead Letter," as he thought this would never be used?
questions.questionHtml: Which article was referred to by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the "Dead Letter," as he thought this would never be used?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Article 356.

Key Points

  • Article 356 of the Indian Constitution allows the President to impose President's Rule in a state if the state government fails to function according to the provisions of the Constitution.
  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar referred to Article 356 as a "Dead Letter," expressing skepticism about its practical application.
  • This provision is invoked when the constitutional machinery in a state breaks down, requiring intervention from the central government.
  • Despite Ambedkar's doubts, Article 356 has been used multiple times in India's history, often criticized for political misuse.
  • It was first invoked in 1951 in Punjab and has since been a contentious aspect of India's federal system.

Additional Information

  • President's Rule: When Article 356 is invoked, the state legislature is either dissolved or suspended, and the Governor takes over the administration under the guidance of the central government.
  • Conditions for Invocation: The President can impose President's Rule based on a report from the Governor or if he/she is satisfied that the state cannot function constitutionally.
  • Duration: President's Rule can initially be imposed for six months and can be extended for a maximum of three years, subject to parliamentary approval every six months.
  • Controversies: The provision has been criticized for being used as a political tool to dismiss state governments led by opposition parties.
  • Recommendations by Commissions: The Sarkaria Commission and the Punchhi Commission have recommended stricter guidelines to prevent misuse of Article 356.

questions.question: The pattern of planetary winds does not largely depend on which of the following factors?
questions.questionHtml: The pattern of planetary winds does not largely depend on which of the following factors?

options.html: Latitudinal variation of atmospheric heating

options.text: The migration of belts following apparent path of the sun
options.html: The migration of belts following apparent path of the sun

options.text: The distribution of continents and oceans

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Topography of mountain ranges.

Key Points

  • The pattern of planetary winds is influenced by factors such as latitudinal variation in atmospheric heating, the distribution of continents and oceans, and the migration of wind belts
  • Mountain topography does not play a significant role in determining the global pattern of planetary winds; its impact is more localized and limited to regional climatic conditions.
  • Global wind systems, such as trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies, are primarily driven by the Earth's rotation and differential heating across latitudes.
  • The Coriolis effect caused by Earth's rotation influences the direction of planetary winds but does not depend on mountainous topography.
  • Factors like pressure belts, the Earth's axial tilt, and the thermal equator have a far greater influence on planetary wind patterns than regional landforms like mountain ranges.

Additional Information

  • Planetary Winds: These are large-scale wind systems that circulate around the globe, including trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies.
  • Coriolis Effect: The deflection of wind direction due to Earth's rotation, influencing the formation of global wind patterns.
  • Pressure Belts: These are zones of high and low pressure across the Earth, such as the equatorial low-pressure belt and subtropical high-pressure belt, which drive wind systems.
  • Thermal Equator: The region receiving the most direct sunlight, shifting seasonally and affecting the migration of wind belts.
  • Localized Impact of Mountain Ranges: While mountain ranges can impact local wind patterns through phenomena like orographic lifting, they do not affect global wind systems significantly.

  • Chanalasvamin was an Acharya (teacher) who received a land grant from Prabhavati Gupta, the daughter of Chandragupta II, in the village of Danguna.

questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements about Human Rights Courts in India are correct?

  1. Human Rights Courts are established by the state governments, with the concurrence of the governor.
  2. These courts have statutory backing under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
  3. For every human rights court, the state government appoints a public prosecutor who has practiced law for at least 7 years.
  4. Human Rights Courts operate independently and have no relationship with the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 2 and 3 only. Key Points

  • Statement 1: False. Human Rights Courts are indeed established by the state governments, but with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, not the governor. This part of the statement is misleading and should be revised to reflect the Chief Justice's role. However, based on the options, we’ll consider this statement incorrect.

  • Statement 2: True. Human Rights Courts are created with statutory backing under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which gives them a legal foundation to operate within the judicial framework.

  • Statement 3: True. As per the guidelines, the state government appoints a public prosecutor for each human rights court, and the individual must have practiced law for at least 7 years to be eligible for the role.

  • Statement 4: False. Human Rights Courts are not independent of the NHRC; in fact, they work as part of the broader framework for protecting and enforcing human rights in India, with the NHRC playing a key role in human rights advocacy and enforcement.

questions.question: Which empire's administration is described by the following characteristics? The king held supreme authority, supported by a council of ministers, including high officials like Kumaramatya and Sandhivigrahika. The empire was divided into provinces (bhuktis) and districts (vishayas), with significant decentralization and regional autonomy. Mahapratihara was the chief of the palace guards. The army was paid in cash, and an officer-in-charge of stores was called Ranabhandagarika.
questions.questionHtml:
Which empire's administration is described by the following characteristics?

  1. The king held supreme authority, supported by a council of ministers, including high officials like Kumaramatya and Sandhivigrahika.
  2. The empire was divided into provinces (bhuktis) and districts (vishayas), with significant decentralization and regional autonomy.
  3. Mahapratihara was the chief of the palace guards.
  4. The army was paid in cash, and an officer-in-charge of stores was called Ranabhandagarika.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Gupta Administration.

Key Points

  • The Gupta administration was highly centralized, with the emperor holding supreme authority and making key decisions about the state’s policies.
  • The empire was organized hierarchically, with a clear division between central, provincial, and military administration.
  • At the central level, the emperor, often considered divine, was assisted by a Council of Ministers, and the bureaucracy had various officials like the kumaramatyas and Mahapratihara.
  • The provincial level saw the empire divided into bhuktis (divisions) and vishayas (districts), with local governance carried out by appointed officials like Uparikas and Vishayapatis.
  • In the military level, the Gupta king led the army during wartime, with specific officials overseeing various aspects of the army such as elephants, horses, and foot soldiers.
  • Revenue generation was primarily from land taxes, supplemented by taxes on trade, and the empire had a regular system for collecting land revenue.
  • The judicial system was well-defined, with the king as the highest authority, assisted by the Mahanandanayaka (Chief Justice), and local disputes were handled by village headmen or provincial officers.

 Additional Information

  • Feudal System and Vassals
    • The Gupta administration incorporated a feudal system, where vassals, often local rulers or chiefs, were given autonomy in exchange for tribute and military service.
    • These vassals were often granted land and other privileges, such as land grants and exemption from taxes, especially to religious leaders.
  • Revenue and Land Grants
    • The land grant system was a major feature of Gupta governance, where religious leaders and administrators were given lands free of tax.
    • This system helped maintain the loyalty of local leaders and promoted agriculture and religious establishments.
  • Military Organization
    • The Gupta army was well-organized, with officers overseeing specific units like elephants, horses, and foot soldiers.
    • The Gupta kings were expected to lead the army in times of war, ensuring strong military leadership.
  • Judicial System
    • The judicial system under the Gupta rulers was sophisticated, with a clear distinction between criminal and civil laws.
    • Local disputes were often handled by village headmen, while more serious cases were dealt with at the provincial and central levels.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the Comptroller Auditor General is INCORRECT?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements regarding the Comptroller Auditor General is INCORRECT?

options.text: He certifies the net proceeds of any tax or duty, which is final.
options.html: He certifies the net proceeds of any tax or duty, which is final.

options.text: He conducts audits of expenditure on behalf of the parliament.
options.html: He conducts audits of expenditure on behalf of the parliament.

options.text: His legal and regulatory audits are discretionary, but his propriety audit is obligatory.
options.html: His legal and regulatory audits are discretionary, but his propriety audit is obligatory.

options.text: Secret services expenditure is outside the purview of CAG.
options.html: Secret services expenditure is outside the purview of CAG.

questions.solution:
The incorrect statement is His legal and regulatory audits are discretionary, but his propriety audit is obligatory.

Key Points

Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India:

Constitutional Provisions:

  • Article 148: The Constitution of India provides for the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India.

  • Guardian of Public Purse: The CAG is responsible for overseeing the entire financial system of the country at both the central and state levels.

Appointment and Term:

  • Appointment: The CAG is appointed by the President of India by a warrant under his hand and seal.

  • Oath/Affirmation: Before taking office, the CAG swears an oath to uphold the Constitution, sovereignty, and integrity of India, and to perform his duties faithfully.

  • Term: The CAG serves for 6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.

  • Resignation and Removal: The CAG can resign at any time by addressing the resignation to the President. He can only be removed on grounds of misbehavior or incapacity through a resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament with a special majority, similar to the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge.

Independence of the CAG:

The Constitution ensures the CAG's independence through the following provisions:

  1. Security of Tenure: The CAG cannot be removed at the pleasure of the President; removal is governed by a specified procedure.

  2. No Further Office: After leaving office, the CAG is not eligible for any further office under the Government of India or any state.

  3. Salary and Service Conditions: The salary of the CAG is equal to that of a Supreme Court judge and cannot be altered to his disadvantage after appointment.

  4. Administrative Expenses: The administrative expenses of the CAG’s office, including salaries and pensions, are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India and do not require Parliament’s vote.

  5. No Ministerial Responsibility: No minister is responsible for the actions of the CAG in Parliament.

Duties and Powers:

  • Audit of Accounts:

    • Audits the accounts of the Union Government, State Governments, and Union Territories with legislative assemblies.

    • Audits the Consolidated Fund of India, Contingency Fund, and Public Accounts.

    • Audits accounts of Government Companies and Corporations substantially financed by the government.

  • Receipts and Expenditures:

    • Ensures that revenue and expenditure are correctly allocated and that funds are used in accordance with legal provisions.

  • Certifications:

    • Certifies the net proceeds of any tax or duty, which is considered final.

  • Advisory Role: The CAG acts as a guide, friend, and philosopher to the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament.

  • Audit Reports: Submits audit reports on:

    • Appropriation Accounts: Compares actual expenditure with approved expenditure.

    • Finance Accounts: Shows the annual receipts and disbursements of the Union government.

    • Public Undertakings: Conducts audits of government-owned corporations.

Role of CAG:

  • Constitutional and Legal Compliance: The CAG ensures that government expenditure is in line with the Constitution and parliamentary laws.

  • Independence in Audit: The CAG has the freedom to decide the scope of audit for government expenditure. However, in audits of receipts, stores, and stock, the approval of the executive government is required.

  • Propriety Audit: The CAG can review the wisdom, economy, and faithfulness of government expenditures (propriety audit), though this is discretionary, not obligatory.

  • His legal and regulatory audits are obligatory, but his propriety audit is discretionary.

    •  Hence, statement 3 is INCORRECT.

 Limitations:

  • Secret Service Expenditure: The CAG does not audit secret service expenditure. Instead, he relies on a certificate from the concerned authority.

  • Comptroller Role: Unlike the CAG of Britain, the CAG of India is only an Auditor-General and does not control the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund. In India, the executive can withdraw money without the CAG’s prior approval.

Audit of Public Corporations and Companies:

  1. Direct Audit: Some corporations, like ONGC, Air India, and Damodar Valley Corporation, are directly audited by the CAG.

  2. Supplementary Audit: The CAG may conduct a supplementary audit of certain corporations that are audited by private professional auditors (e.g., Central Warehousing Corporation, Industrial Finance Corporation).

  3. Private Audit: Some corporations are audited entirely by private auditors without CAG involvement, such as LIC, RBI, SBI, and Food Corporation of India.

  4. Government Companies: The CAG may conduct supplementary or test audits for government companies that are privately audited.

Establishment of Audit Board (1968):

  • An Audit Board was created to handle specialized audits, such as those related to engineering, iron and steel, and chemicals.

  • The board consists of a Chairman and two members appointed by the CAG.

Consider the following statements regarding Nickel:

I. India’s nickel reserves are predominantly found in sulphide deposits in the Western Ghats.

II. Nickel plays a major role in clean energy technologies, especially in electric vehicle batteries.

III. A recent study indicates that nickel can be extracted from low-grade ores using hydrogen plasma instead of carbon.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2.

In News

  • A new study has reported that nickel can now be extracted from low-grade ores using hydrogen plasma, offering a greener alternative to carbon-based smelting techniques.

Key Points

  • Statement I: In India, nickel occurs mainly as oxides, sulphides, and silicates, but India's substantial reserves are in the form of laterites, especially in Odisha’s Sukinda region, not in sulphide form in the Western Ghats. Hence, Statement I is incorrect.
  • Statement II: Nickel is used in clean energy technologies, particularly in electric vehicle batteries, including nickel-metal hydride and nickel-cadmium batteries. Hence, Statement II is correct.
  • Statement III: A recent study confirms that hydrogen plasma can be used to extract nickel from low-grade ores instead of conventional carbon-based methods. Hence, Statement III is correct.

Additional Information

  • Symbol: Ni
  • Atomic Number: 28
  • Major reserve-holding countries: Indonesia, Australia, Brazil, Russia, Cuba, Philippines.
  • Major use: Stainless steel production, battery technologies, and heat-resistant alloys.
